name: Amira Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy medical supplies, gloves, dressings, syringes and test kits, for a distributor that serves pharmacies and small clinics. I start at eight with the stock report, and by nine I'm on the phone with a manufacturer about a late shipment. Mid-morning I check expiry dates, because a batch that goes out of date is real money and real risk. Afternoons are meetings and fixing other people's mistakes. I'm good at it, but I'm tired of being the one who has to catch everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, nothing to see. Between us colleagues we'd have a laugh about the last big AI promise that fizzled. I'd stay out of the online arguments, they just wind people up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still feel uneasy. The firm is under pressure from bigger competitors, my savings would last about three months, and I'm 58. If the company cuts costs, it'll be me or someone like me, because we're the highly paid ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep my head down and do the job well. I'd put away a little more each month and check my pension forecast, which I've been avoiding. I'd also keep my paper checklists for expiry dates, because the system has missed a few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is the right word. It's not about AI, it's about the firm and the money. I've seen two rounds of redundancies in my time and the senior people weren't safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on. What would worry you even in that quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our finance director, Mr Okafor, wants a lower wage bill every year. Last spring the stock team lost two people and nobody said why. If they do it again, I'd be in the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you talk to about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Lena, who's been here as long as I have. We trust each other. We'd compare what we've heard and not trust the official line.

say: I'd say there's **nothing to see** and laugh about the last overhyped promise.
I'd stay out of **online arguments**, since they wind people up.
think: My savings last **three months**, and as a highly paid senior I'm a cost target.
The worry comes from the **firm's pressure**, not from AI.
do: Carry on and do the job **well**.
Add a little more to my **pension** and finally check the forecast.
Keep my **paper checklists** for expiry dates.
feel: **Uneasy**, about the firm and the money rather than AI.
S0.quote: I've seen two rounds of redundancies in my time and the senior people weren't safe either.
fieldNote: She carries **money worry** that has nothing to do with AI, and reads quiet years through past redundancies.
She distrusts **official lines**, and prefers comparing notes with a trusted colleague.

steps.text: Check the pension forecast I've been avoiding
Keep paper checklists for batch expiry dates
Put away a little more each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'd tell my manager that the system must be proven on small orders before I trust it. And I'd say to friends that whoever sells these tools will say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried. A large part of my work is checking and ordering, the exact things on that card. I'm slow with new tools and I know it. If the firm moves fast, I'm exposed, even though I'm one of the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay useful where it counts: expiry risk, supplier problems, anything where a mistake matters. I'd ask for training only if they promise it's safe. I'd also put 400 a month into savings and talk with Raj about what we'd do if I went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have some control, but I don't like it. Every week I'd worry about a new announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your buying tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine reorders. Anything repeating each month. A machine will do it faster, and honestly, mostly right. Where it goes wrong is the odd order, a shortage or a recall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the company asked you to use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them, because I'm not stupid, but I'd hold my ground on checking the outputs. I won't have a machine placing orders for sterile supplies without a human check. If they pushed past that, I'd go to the compliance officer.

say: I'd tell my manager the system must be **proven on small orders** first.
I'd tell friends whoever sells these tools **will say anything**.
think: Much of my work is **checking and ordering**, and I'm slow with new tools.
Even as one of the best I'm **exposed** if the firm moves fast.
do: Stay useful in **expiry risk** and supplier problems.
Talk with Raj about what we'd do if I **went**.
feel: **Anxious**, with some control but little trust in the pace.
S1.quote: I won't have a machine placing orders for sterile supplies without a human check.
fieldNote: She is **honest about being slow**, but sets a hard safety line she would take to the compliance officer.
Her worry is **concrete**, about being exposed, even though she is among the best.

steps.text: Focus on expiry risk and supplier problems where mistakes matter
Insist on a human check for sterile supply orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and nobody is ready. I'd tell my manager that the firm must give us notice, in writing. And to friends, I'd say, vote for people with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be out. The thinking part of my job is all of it, the robots take three years more, but by then I'd be gone. At 58, getting a new job is harder, and the savings won't stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending the first week, everything non-essential. I'd ask for a meeting about early retirement and a payout. I'd go to the pension adviser, whom I've avoided, and see what I'd get at 60. And I'd talk to Raj about giving up the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me awake. I already don't sleep well. I'd have bills, the mortgage, and Raj's school, which can't carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the holiday and the small treats first. Then the second car. Then maybe we'd look at selling and renting. I don't want to, but I'd rather decide than be forced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be exposed. What would that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj's driving school makes very little, mostly lessons in the evening. If I lost my pay, we'd survive a few months, not years. The kids could help a little, but I'd hate to ask.

say: I'd tell my manager the firm must give us **notice in writing**.
I'd tell friends to **vote for people** with a plan.
think: I think I'd be **out**, and at 58 a new job is hard.
My savings would **not stretch**, and Raj's school can't carry us.
do: Ask for an **early-retirement** meeting and a payout.
Go to the **pension adviser** and see what 60 would give.
feel: **Alarmed**, and awake at night over bills.
S2.quote: I'd rather decide than be forced.
fieldNote: She is **alarmed and practical**, moving quickly to spending cuts and the pension adviser.
The **household has little slack**: Raj's income is small and the savings are about three months.

steps.text: Cut the holiday, small treats and the second car
Ask for an early-retirement meeting and a payout
See the pension adviser about what 60 would give
Talk with Raj about selling and renting if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a lot of change and I'd ask for a plan from the company. I'd say five years isn't enough for people my age to do anything but hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's better, but not much. I'd be 63, and still not retired, with the thinking part of my job done by machines. The extra time just lets me watch it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to pay down the mortgage and build six months of savings. I'd plan to retire at 62, not 65, accepting the smaller pension. I'd also train my junior colleague so I leave something behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though less so than with two years. It's a slow dread, not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years should feel better. Does it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much help. A decade ago I could have learned something new, now it takes me longer. I'm honest with myself about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena to look for a plan of her own. We'd stay in touch. If either of us hears anything, we'd tell the other.

say: I'd ask the company for **a plan**.
I'd say five years is not enough for people my age to **do much**.
think: It's better than two years, but I'd be **63 and not retired** when it lands.
The extra time lets me **watch it come**.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** and build six months of savings.
Plan to retire at **62** and accept a smaller pension.
feel: **Alarmed** but slower, a dread rather than a shock.
S3.quote: The extra time just lets me watch it come.
fieldNote: She sees extra time as **a way** to finish her money plan, not to learn new skills.
She is **honest about her pace** and clear that a decade earlier she might have retrained.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage and build six months of savings
Retire at 62 on a smaller pension
Train a junior colleague to take over my accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and the world will change in ways we can't see now. I'd say we should check the claims. People said robots would take our jobs forty years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired, so it's not my fight. But I'd worry for my kids and the younger staff, who'd still be in the thick of it. Uneasy in a distant way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62, retire with a modest pension, and use the time to keep my savings safe. I'd help the juniors with whatever I can, but I'm not an activist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for others. Ten years feels like plenty, and I'd sleep better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter works in a bank and my son in a hospital. I'd tell them to keep their skills current and not to count on pensions. And not to trust a company just because it says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people who come after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave detailed notes on how I handle recalls and expiry, so that the knowledge stays. It's small, but it's what I can do.

say: I'd say **check the claims**, because people said robots would take jobs forty years ago.
I'd say the world will change in ways we can't see yet.
think: I'd be **retired by then**, so it's not my fight.
I'd worry for my **kids and younger staff**, who'd still be in the thick of it.
do: Work to **62** and retire on a modest pension.
Leave **detailed notes** on how I handle recalls and expiry.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for others, and sleeping better.
S4.quote: I'd leave detailed notes on how I handle recalls and expiry, so that the knowledge stays.
fieldNote: With ten years her concern moves to her **children** and the juniors, and she stays modest about what she can do.
She is **sceptical by history**, recalling earlier predictions that robots would take jobs.

steps.text: Work until 62 then retire on a modest pension
Write detailed notes on recalls and expiry handling
Tell my grown children to keep their skills current

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The five-year and two-year ones both scare me, but I'd pick two years, since I'd have no time to get ready. I'm 58, I have maybe three months saved, and Raj's driving school is slow. What would help is simple: notice, a decent payout, and someone at the firm who tells us the truth early. I don't need a retraining course, I need to reach my pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm against everything new. I'm not, I just want it to be proven. If it's safe and it works, fine. I won't be the one to test it on live orders.

headlineQuote: If it's safe and it works, fine. I won't be the one to test it on live orders.
portrait: **Amira** is 58, a senior buyer of medical supplies for a distributor serving pharmacies and small clinics.
She is **pragmatic and resistant**, never uses AI tools, and wants anything new proven before it touches live orders.
In the political middle, she **blames no one** in particular, but distrusts promises from managers and vendors.
With about **three months saved** and a partner whose driving school is slow, her margin for error is small.
Her worry climbs fast as time shrinks, and she wants **notice** and a payout more than retraining.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, since she'd have no time to prepare before her pension.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **early notice** and a decent payout, and an honest message from management.
